name: Kansas Reflector
title: Lack of major property tax relief in Kansas prompts fingerpointing in governor’s race
text:
Democrat Cindy Holscher and Republican Ty Masterson appear at the Sept. 12, 2026, debate at the Kansas State Fair. The two rivals for governor agree on the need to reduce property taxes for homeowners but clash on the details. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Kansas Senate President Ty Masterson shared with television viewers Jan. 12, 2021, a vision for how Republicans could deal with runaway property taxes.
In the GOP reply to Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly’s State of the State speech, Masterson promised GOP lawmakers would address the burden of $5.4 billion in property taxes collected statewide at that time. It wasn’t an unimaginable political feat given Masterson’s authority over the GOP supermajority in the Senate and House Speaker Dan Hawkins’ control of the two-thirds Republican majority in the House.
It was a politically astute pledge, because polling consistently affirmed property tax applied to homeowners was the most hated, relative to sales and income taxes.
“We must work to enact meaningful property tax reform to allow seniors and families to stay in their homes,” Masterson vowed.
Senate President Ty Masterson, the 2026 Republican nominee for governor, promises in a 2021 video message to make property tax reform a top legislative priority. (Kansas Reflector screen capture of Kansas Legislature video)
The Legislature spent the next five years nibbling on the edge of reform, but annual statewide revenue from property taxes ballooned to $6.6 billion by 2025. Legislators continued to hear from folks outraged by double-digit escalation of property valuations that triggered tax increases even when mill levies remained flat.
Sen. Cindy Holscher, the Democratic Party’s nominee for governor, said Masterson and Hawkins failed to leverage their Republican supermajorities to grapple with property taxes in the manner they did to slash state income taxes and trim the state’s sales tax on groceries. In the 2026 legislative session, the House and Senate ran into gridlock as they took turns voting down competing GOP property tax bills.
“Ty Masterson has had years as Senate president, with a Republican supermajority behind him, and time and again he has repeatedly failed to deliver the property tax relief Kansans need,” Holscher said. “He said, ‘We can do whatever we want because we’re in charge.’ He either doesn’t want to do this or doesn’t know how.”
Masterson, the Republican gubernatorial nominee, joined the outcry. He said he was disappointed obstinate Democrats and “phony Republicans” stood in the way of efforts to limit the ability of school, city and county officials to pile up property tax revenue.
“The truth of why your taxes are so high … people like Cindy have not met one of your tax dollars she didn’t want to spend two of. You have to put constraints on the local government,” Masterson said. “I want to make your life more affordable and property taxes is a big part of that.”
In 1997, residential property owners in Kansas accounted for 38% of property tax revenue, while commercial property owners picked up 62%. The accumulation of tax exemptions for businesses reversed the math. By 2024, residential owners paid 57% of the property tax bill in Kansas and commercial property owners in the state covered 43%.
 
The track record
The Legislature during the past five years considered dozens of ideas for modifying the property tax landscape, but momentum for reform was tempered by the reality that local government received the majority of its funding from property tax. Cities and counties objected to the Legislature wading into their funding stream.
In 2021, the Legislature approved a “truth in taxation” law preventing cities, counties or townships from raising property tax revenue above the previous year’s inflation-adjusted total without mailing advance notice to taxpayers and conducting public hearings before voting on property tax changes.
State lawmakers in 2022 agreed to provide property tax reimbursements to retail business owners subjected to shutdown orders during the COVID-19 pandemic. Attempts by the Legislature to implement vehicle property tax relief prompted vetoes by Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly. Legislators did raise the residential exemption on property taxes to fund K-12 public schools from $20,000 to $40,000. That saved the average homeowner about $46 per year. Meanwhile, the Legislature approved property tax exemptions for telecommunications equipment.
In 2023, lawmakers debated, but failed to pass, an amendment to the Kansas Constitution to cap growth in property valuations that were the cause of higher tax bills for many homeowners.
In 2024, Kelly signed a measure raising the residential property tax exemption to $75,000 when calculating the 20-mill levy for aid to K-12 public schools. The Legislature’s focus that year was on cutting state income taxes. During a special session, the Legislature and governor agreed to a $1.2 billion, three-year reduction.
The Legislature voted in 2025 to eliminate 1.5 mills of state property tax levies relied on to finance state building construction projects. But that $80 million annual reduction in state property tax collections did nothing to change the reality that local governments continued to depend on property taxes for the vast majority of operating revenue. Kansas did adopt a property tax exemption in 2025 for off-road vehicles, boats and trailers.
In 2026, the House and Senate clashed for months without finding consensus on a sweeping property tax fix.
With Masterson’s blessing, the Senate tried to bulldoze through the legislative process an amendment to the Kansas Constitution limiting increases in annual assessment of property values to 3%. The House declined to endorse that approach. Instead, the House sought to prevent local units of government from increasing revenue from property taxes by more than 3% annually. Amid that debate, proposals calling for phasing out the property tax and replacing that revenue with a higher sales tax floundered.
Kelly vetoed a bill in the 2026 session that would have capped city and county spending increases at 3% or the rate of inflation and would have authorized Kansans to file signature petitions to block local property tax increases above that threshold. The governor dismissed the measure as evidence of the legislative leadership’s “false promise” of meaningful property tax reform.
Instead, she encouraged the Legislature to double to $150,000 the portion of a home’s value not subject to property taxes for schools. She recommended creation of a $60 million state fund to reward cities or counties that held budget increases to less than 3%.
 
Sen. Cindy Holscher says many of the Republicans’ ideas for property tax cuts amount to “gimmicks.” (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)
Plans for change
Masterson, who has said during the governor’s race that property tax reform was a top priority, offered voters a “Homeowners Bill of Rights” that would guide the Republican if he were elected governor Nov. 3.
The blueprint would be anchored by a constitutional amendment to cap at 3% annual growth in the valuation of taxable property. In the alternative, the amendment would enable the Legislature to impose a limit on property tax rates. Constitutional amendments require consent from two-thirds of the House and Senate before placed on a statewide ballot.
“I have a neighbor. He’s spending more than double the property tax alone than he had been for his entire mortgage, interest, insurance taxes combined,” Masterson said. “At the same time, that’s putting such a load on our young people to afford housing, and homeownership is the underpinning of the middle class of any country. Our first-time average homeowner is now close to 40, and that’s just not acceptable.”
Masterson, who has represented Andover in the Legislature for 20 years, said he wanted local taxing jurisdictions to secure direct voter consent for “unreasonable” budget increases linked to property tax revenue. He would freeze or reduce property taxes for senior citizens and work toward inhibiting Kansans from being “taxed out” of a home, farm or business.
Holscher, an Overland Park resident elected to the Legislature in 2016, said much of the GOP’s strategy for property tax reform amount to “gimmicks” or concepts designed to financially starve local governments responsible for delivering essential public services.
“They squeeze the balloon, they shuffle the responsibility somewhere else, and it makes it harder for our local levels to raise the revenue they need for their critical services,” she said.
Holscher recommended the Legislature provide funding to fully meet its obligation to finance special education programs in K-12 public schools. When the state avoided its responsibility to students, she said, local school boards were forced to dip deeper into property tax revenue to cover program costs.
“Special education hasn’t been fully funded since 2011,” she said. “We’re federally mandated to fund it. When we don’t do that, that burden gets shifted to the local level.”
The Democratic senator said Kansas ought to lower the taxed percentage of home values from 11.5% to 9%, which would deliver property tax relief to homeowners across all income levels. In addition, Holscher recommended restraining the issuance of tax breaks to wealthy business owners. She also support specific property tax exemptions for seniors and disabled veterans.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Commentary: A tale of a law, a lawsuit and many missed opportunities for Kentucky children
text:
The Kentucky Court of Appeals in Frankfort, Kentucky, on Oct. 23, 2026. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Sarah Ladd)At 2:30 Saturday morning, I woke up troubled by the October 23 hearing in the Kentucky Court of Appeals that I had attended.
One thought kept returning: We shouldn’t have been in that courtroom at all.
I had listened as attorneys debated subpoenas, funding, the State Auditor’s authority and whether the dispute was moot. How had a kinship care law intended to protect vulnerable children brought us to this point?
My thoughts returned to a conversation with a grandmother in 2019.
When her grandson was removed from his home, she took him in. She signed paperwork without fully understanding how that decision could affect financial assistance for his care.
She later realized she had potentially waived access to thousands of dollars of assistance. 
I shared her concerns with a senior Cabinet for Health and Family Services official, who acknowledged communication could improve, but maintained the process was legal.
In my view, communication fell short. And something can be legal and still need to change.
That experience helped lead to Senate Bill (SB) 151, unanimously passed by Kentucky’s General Assembly in 2024 and signed by Governor Andy Beshear.
The law established a 120-day window for relatives and fictive kin to understand their options and pursue approval as kinship foster parents. It allowed caregivers experiencing qualifying events to seek reconsideration for foster care approval—potentially keeping children in the same home with support.
It also strengthened opportunities for children to identify relatives or trusted adults they wanted considered for placement.
Then implementation stalled.
The administration cited Fletcher v. Commonwealth, a Kentucky Supreme Court decision concerning legislative appropriations, to justify waiting for additional funding.
CHFS initially estimated implementation at $20 million, later revising that figure to $14.6 million annually. Both estimates relied entirely on state General Fund dollars, despite SB 151’s direction to maximize available federal funding.
I believed Kentucky had other funding options and that portions of the law could have moved forward while financial questions were resolved.
Instead, families waited.
That’s why I asked State Auditor Allison Ball in 2024 to independently examine the funding assumptions behind the delay.
What followed was a legal battle over the Auditor’s authority to obtain information.
Ball sued Governor Beshear and CHFS. The Cabinet maintained it had cooperated with her investigation; Ball argued she lacked information necessary to complete it.
Franklin Circuit Court Judge Thomas Wingate dismissed the lawsuit as premature, citing, in part, the Auditor’s failure to use subpoenas.
On appeal, Ball argued that routinely requiring subpoenas could undermine independent oversight. She cited KRS 43.080, requiring agencies to permit access to records upon the Auditor’s request.
After nearly 30 years in government, I understand what may feel like burdensome information requests. But genuine cooperation means providing what you can and establishing reasonable timelines—avoiding the appearance of a standoff.
If agencies decide what information is sufficient for an independent audit, how independent is that oversight?
Ball warned that without meaningful access to information, her office could become an “empty shell.”  There are implications far beyond SB 151.
In July 2026, CHFS began implementing SB 151 after the General Assembly appropriated $12 million over two years.
The Cabinet now argues that implementation makes the appeal moot.
Really? Moot to whom?
Beginning implementation two years later doesn’t answer whether the original funding estimates were accurate, whether federal funding opportunities and alternative approaches were adequately explored, or whether portions of the law could have been implemented sooner.  
Nor does it restore opportunities lost by families in 2024 and 2025.  
These are questions, not accusations, but answers matter—especially when the full implementation of a law intended to protect vulnerable children was delayed for two years.
In March 2026, a proposed administrative regulation was found deficient following legislative review. I testified, raising concerns about the approach and absence of federal funding.
Then HB 500, the 2026 budget legislation, incorporated language from the proposed regulation, and CHFS proceeded through internal policy.
Questions remain about whether that approach fulfills SB 151’s intent and whether state funding is sustainable. To my knowledge, there is still no approved implementing regulation. I continue working with legislators, CHFS and the Auditor’s office to seek answers.
Meanwhile, children still need their voices heard.
Days before the appeal, I advocated for a teenage foster youth who was in three homes in five days. Although his social worker reportedly had arranged his latest placement days earlier, I was told he learned about the last move when transportation arrived after football practice to take him there. 
SB 151 was intended to strengthen children’s voices in placement decisions.
Was that promise moot to him?
We cannot always change what brings children into the child welfare system. But we can change how government responds.
And that brings me back to the courtroom.
There I sat, a kinship caregiver and advocate, watching State Auditor Allison Ball herself stand at the podium, defending her authority to obtain information.
Our fight began with children and families who deserved better. But it had grown beyond SB 151. The independence of an office responsible for government oversight was now at stake.
The court will decide the legal questions. But the consequences of government decisions don’t disappear when a lawsuit ends.
We don’t need empty shells. We need laws that deliver on all their promises and independent oversight to ensure accountability.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Virginia lawmakers approve plan to advance new K-12 school funding formula
text:
A cup of pencils sit on top of a classroom desk in a Virginia school. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)A state legislative subcommittee on Monday approved a plan to hire an expert to study a new school funding formula for Virginia, with up to 24 months to complete the work.
The decision continues lawmakers’ work to update the state’s 52-year-old funding formula, which determines the Standards of Quality, or funding level for public schools. A December 2023 study showed that Virginia local governments spend far more on K-12 education than the state, underscoring the need for a clearer approach.
Virginia Dept. of Ed projects K-12 schools will need $1.2 billion over next two years

Researchers from the Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission, which studied the formula, said lawmakers could partially replace the SOQ formula by using student-based calculations for special education and English learner funding. Another option would be to fully replace the entire staffing-based formula with a new student-based formula, researchers said.
Sen. Mamie Locke, D-Hampton, who was re-elected chair of the Joint Subcommittee to Study Elementary and Secondary Education Funding on Monday, said that although the group has 24 months, it would be “optimal” to complete the work when Gov. Abigail Spanberger presents her biennium budget requests in December 2027.
“I don’t think it’s going to take us 24 months to get this work done, and that would be better and in the best interest of our school districts and our kids if we can move this as quickly as possible,” Locke said.
The scope of work requires the consultant to give lawmakers a data-driven tool to evaluate alternative K–12 funding formulas and understand their fiscal and distributional impacts before implementing changes.
Holly Coy, chief of staff for the Virginia Department of Education, said that once the agency finalizes the draft Request for Proposal, or formal service request, it will publish the proposal and accept bids for 30 days. 
The agency expects to select a consultant and begin work during the upcoming General Assembly session in January.
Coy said lawmakers will have an opportunity after the session to provide further input to the consultant on the policy factors that will be built into the funding model. 
Factors include base funding per student, extra weights for student needs, class sizes, operating costs, transition provisions, and the Local Composite Index, which determines what each locality can pay for its schools.
Virginia has increased ongoing K–12 education funding by just over $4 billion, or 50%, from fiscal year 2023 to fiscal year 2028, according to a staff report for the subcommittee, highlighted by $1.5 billion in teacher salaries, plus $375.4 million in one-time educator bonuses.
Other investments include $273.2 million in additional funding for at-risk students, $537.5 million in additional funding for school support staff, $126.8 million to establish and expand dedicated funding for special education, and $106.9 million for additional English language learner teachers and reading specialists positions.
The state has also contributed to additional funding for school construction, early childhood education, and updates to school funding calculations.
Del. Cia Price, D-Newport News, a committee member, expressed support for moving the matter forward without further delay.
“I think this is overdue, and so anything that we can do one time thoughtfully and expeditiously… I think just to put on the record our desire for this to go aggressively, thoughtfully, quickly,” she said.
